title: Logistic regression
story:
The difficulty is a mismatch of ranges. A linear combination of inputs can return any real number at all, and the thing you want back is a probability, which is confined between zero and one. Fit the line directly to labels of zero and one and it will cheerfully predict 1.4 for a confident case and negative numbers for others, and there is no sensible way to read those.

The fix is to move the problem somewhere the line fits. Take the odds — the probability divided by one minus itself — and then the logarithm of that. The result runs over the whole real line: certainty in one direction goes to positive infinity, certainty in the other to negative infinity, and even chances sit at zero. Now a linear model is at home, and you map back through the inverse when you want a probability again.

The curve doing the mapping is older than this use of it. Verhulst introduced the logistic equation in 1838, in a note on the law population follows in its growth — exponential growth with a ceiling on it, fitted to the populations of several countries — and named the solution the logistic curve in a later paper. The work was then forgotten and rediscovered in the 1920s. Berkson brought it to this problem in 1944, applying the logistic function to bio-assay and coining the term logit, from logistic unit, as a simpler and more computationally efficient alternative to the probit model then in use. Cox gave the general regression treatment in 1958, for a sequence of zeros and ones where the chance that a trial is a one may depend on one or more independent variables, read before the Research Section in March of that year.

Notice that the name is honest, even though it is the piece that confuses people most. This is regression — a linear model, fitted by maximum likelihood — that happens to be used for classification because its output can be thresholded. The linearity is real and it is in the log-odds, not in the probability.

That last distinction is where the interpretation lives. A coefficient says that a one-unit change in its input adds a fixed amount to the log-odds. Because the logistic curve is steep in the middle and flat at both ends, the same fixed amount corresponds to a large change in probability near even odds and almost none out where the model is already confident. So a coefficient is not an effect on probability, and quoting it as though it were is the most common way this model gets misreported.

problem.name: Log-odds regression
problem.shape: A linear model has to produce a probability, and linear functions are not confined to the interval a probability lives in.
tell: the target is binary and a linear fit is being considered
predicted values fall outside zero and one
coefficients are being read as changes in probability
a decision threshold is being applied to a continuous score
problem.move: Model the log-odds linearly and map back through the logistic curve, fitting by maximum likelihood rather than least squares. Report effects as changes in odds, or convert to probability at a stated baseline, and choose the decision threshold separately from the fit because it encodes the relative cost of the two errors.
problem.invariant: The model is linear in the log-odds and never in the probability. Every interpretation of a coefficient is an interpretation on that scale.
problem.breaks: The same coefficient means different things at different places on the curve, because the mapping back is nonlinear and flat at both ends — so an effect that is large near even odds is almost invisible where the model is already confident, and an average marginal effect hides that variation rather than summarising it.

cost.time: no closed form, so the fit is iterative, though the likelihood is concave and the optimisation is well behaved
cost.space: one coefficient per feature, which keeps the fitted model inspectable
cost.beats: fitting a line directly to the labels, which predicts impossible values and whose errors are neither normal nor of constant variance

worked.problem: What goes wrong if you just fit a straight line to labels that are zeros and ones?
worked.reasoning:
Four things, and only the first is the one people mention.

The predictions leave the interval. A linear function is unbounded, so for inputs at the extremes it returns values above one and below zero, and those cannot be read as probabilities. Clipping them is not a repair — it hides the fact that the model was fitted on an objective that considered those values legitimate.

The error structure is wrong for least squares. With a binary outcome the variance of the error depends on the mean: it is largest near even odds and shrinks to nothing as the probability approaches zero or one. Least squares assumes constant variance, so the fit is inefficient and the standard errors it reports are not the ones you want.

The loss saturates in the wrong direction. This is the deepest problem and it is the same point that appears in the treatment of why loss functions take logs. Fitted by maximum likelihood, the loss is the negative log of the predicted probability, and that log undoes the exponential inside the logistic curve, so a confidently wrong prediction produces a large gradient. Fitted by squared error against a bounded output, the loss flattens exactly where the curve flattens, so the worse the model is, the less it learns.

And the shape is wrong in the tails. A straight line keeps going, but the probability of an outcome cannot keep rising with the input forever — real relationships of this kind level off. The logistic curve levels off by construction, which is not a convenience; it is the correct qualitative behaviour.

So the move is to put the linear model where a linear model belongs: on the log-odds, which run over the whole real line. Fit by maximum likelihood, map back through the curve for a probability, and set the decision threshold separately, because where you threshold encodes the relative cost of a false positive against a false negative and has nothing to do with the quality of the fit.

THE MISMATCH

   linear combination  ->  any real number
   probability         ->  [0, 1] only

   fit a line to 0/1 labels and it predicts 1.4
   for a confident case, and negatives elsewhere.

THE MOVE: PUT THE LINE WHERE IT FITS

   odds      =  p / (1 - p)          (0, inf)
   log-odds  =  log( p / (1-p) )     (-inf, inf)

      certain yes  ->  +inf
      even chance  ->    0
      certain no   ->  -inf

   NOW a linear model is at home.
   map back through the logistic curve for a
   probability.

FOUR THINGS WRONG WITH THE STRAIGHT LINE

   1. PREDICTIONS LEAVE THE INTERVAL
        clipping is not a repair -- it hides that
        the objective considered those values
        legitimate.

   2. ERROR VARIANCE IS NOT CONSTANT
        for a binary outcome the variance depends
        on the mean: largest near even odds,
        vanishing at 0 and 1.
        least squares assumes constant variance.

   3. THE LOSS SATURATES THE WRONG WAY   <- deepest
        max likelihood  ->  loss = -log(p)
              the log UNDOES the exp in the curve
              -> confidently wrong = BIG gradient
        squared error against a bounded output
              -> flattens where the curve flattens
              -> the worse it is, the less it learns

   4. THE TAILS ARE THE WRONG SHAPE
        a line keeps going. real relationships of
        this kind LEVEL OFF. the logistic curve
        levels off by construction.

THE INTERPRETATION TRAP

   a coefficient adds a FIXED amount to LOG-ODDS.

   the curve is steep in the middle, flat at the
   ends, so that fixed amount is:

      near even odds   ->  a large change in p
      out at the ends  ->  almost none

   -> a coefficient is NOT an effect on
      probability. quoting it as one is the
      commonest misreport of this model.

AND SET THE THRESHOLD SEPARATELY

   where you cut encodes the relative cost of the
   two errors. it is not part of the fit.

problem.practice: Fit a logistic model and take its largest coefficient. Compute the change in predicted probability that a one-unit change in that input produces, first for a row near even odds and then for a row the model already scores at 0.95. Then fit a plain linear model to the same binary labels and count how many of its predictions fall outside zero and one.

beats.broke: A linear function of the inputs returns any real number, and what you need back is a probability, which exists only between zero and one.
beats.fix: Model the log-odds instead. The logit maps that interval onto the whole real line, so a linear model can be fitted there and mapped back through the logistic curve — a curve introduced in 1838 for bounded population growth, brought to this problem in 1944, and given its general regression treatment in 1958.
beats.cost: The coefficients describe additive changes in log-odds rather than in probability, so the same coefficient means a large effect near even odds and almost none where the model is already confident.

interview.q: What goes wrong if you just fit a straight line to labels that are zeros and ones?
interview.trap: Stopping at predictions outside zero and one. That is the visible symptom; the error variance is not constant, the tails are the wrong shape, and — the one that decides whether it trains — squared error against a bounded output saturates exactly where the curve does.
interview.answer:
Four things, and only the first is the one usually mentioned.

Predictions leave the interval. A linear function is unbounded, so at the extremes it returns values above one and below zero, which cannot be read as probabilities. Clipping them is not a repair; it conceals that the objective treated those values as legitimate.

The error structure is wrong for least squares. With a binary outcome the variance of the error depends on the mean — largest near even odds, vanishing as the probability approaches zero or one — while least squares assumes constant variance, so the fit is inefficient and its standard errors are not the ones you want.

The loss saturates in the wrong direction, which is the deepest issue and the same point that appears in why loss functions take logs. Under maximum likelihood the loss is the negative log of the predicted probability, and that log undoes the exponential inside the logistic curve, so a confidently wrong prediction yields a large gradient. Under squared error against a bounded output the loss flattens exactly where the curve flattens, so the worse the model is, the less it learns.

And the tails are the wrong shape. A straight line keeps rising, but probabilities of this kind level off in reality, and the logistic curve levels off by construction — which is correct qualitative behaviour rather than a convenience.

So the move is to put the linear model where linearity belongs, on the log-odds, fit by maximum likelihood, and map back through the curve. I would also set the decision threshold separately from the fit, because where you cut encodes the relative cost of the two errors and says nothing about how good the model is.

RANGE MISMATCH, AND THE FIX

   linear model     any real number
   probability      [0, 1]

   log-odds = log( p / (1-p) )   ->  (-inf, +inf)

   fit the line THERE. map back through the curve.

THE LINEAGE

   1838  the logistic equation: exponential growth
         with a ceiling, fitted to national
         populations. named later. forgotten,
         rediscovered in the 1920s.
   1944  applied to bio-assay; "logit" coined,
         from LOGISTIC UNIT; offered as simpler
         and cheaper than probit.
   1958  the general regression treatment for
         binary sequences.

WHY NOT A PLAIN LINE ON 0/1 LABELS

   predictions outside [0,1]
   error variance depends on the mean
   loss saturates where the curve flattens
      -> confidently wrong learns SLOWEST
   tails keep rising instead of levelling off

THE INTERPRETATION RULE

   linear in LOG-ODDS. never in probability.

   one coefficient, two very different effects:
      near even odds  -> large change in p
      already confident -> nearly none

   so: report odds, or convert at a stated
   baseline. never quote a coefficient as an
   effect on probability.

SEPARATE CONCERNS

   the FIT           maximum likelihood
   the THRESHOLD     the relative cost of the two
                     errors

   these are not the same decision.
takeaway: The model is linear in the log-odds and never in the probability, which is why the logit exists at all — and why one coefficient means a large effect near even odds and almost nothing where the model is already sure.
